labs.title: Interpret This Output
labs.objective: Given model output, write the business interpretation — the exam's favorite task.
steps: On paper/screen:
Given: logistic regression, coef(income)=0.02 (p<0.001), coef(age)=-0.5 (p=0.03), AUC=0.72, n=5000.
Write: (1) what each coefficient means in plain language, (2) whether the model is useful, (3) one caveat.

Example: 'Each $1k income raises log-odds of purchase by 0.02 (significant); each year of age lowers it by 0.5 (marginally significant). AUC 0.72 = modest discrimination. Caveat: correlation, not causation — and check for confounding by tenure.'
Trade with a peer (or self-review tomorrow): is the interpretation honest?

checks.hint: Confirm AUC interpretation.
Confirm caveats stated.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — interpretation is translation: statistics to decisions. Practice the translation.

labs.title: Choose and Run the Right Test
labs.objective: Match three business questions to their correct tests and run them with assumption checks.
steps: Generate synthetic data with `python3`: (a) order values for mobile vs desktop users (continuous, 2 groups, mildly skewed), (b) device type vs purchase flag (categorical x categorical), (c) order values across mobile/desktop/tablet (3 groups); save to /tmp/dsc_tests.csv with a fixed seed.

Write `/tmp/dsc_tests.py`: for (a) run a Q-Q plot check then choose t-test (or Mann-Whitney U if skew is severe — justify in comments), for (b) chi-square test of independence, for (c) one-way ANOVA; print each test statistic, p-value, AND the effect size (Cohen's d / Cramer's V / eta-squared).
Add the assumption-check comments per test: independence (design), normality/Q-Q for (a), expected cell counts >=5 for (b), equal variances (Levene) for (c) — and what you'd do if each failed.

Write the stakeholder sentence for each result: plain-English verdict + effect size, no p-value worship (e.g., 'desktop orders average $6.20 higher, 95% CI [$3.10, $9.30] — meaningful for the shipping-threshold decision').

checks.output: three tests run with statistics, p-values, effect sizes, assumption notes, and stakeholder sentences
checks.hint: scipy.stats has ttest_ind, chi2_contingency, f_oneway; compute effect sizes manually — that's the learning.

labs.debrief: Test selection is now a decision tree you can run, not a list you memorize — and every result ships with its assumptions checked and its business translation attached.

labs.title: Confidence Intervals and Power, by Simulation
labs.objective: Build intuition for CIs and power by simulating them — watch coverage and detection rates emerge.
steps: Write `/tmp/dsc_sim.py`: simulate 1,000 experiments (two groups, n=50 each, true lift = +0.5 SD); for each, compute the 95% CI of the mean difference and record whether it covers the true lift — print the coverage rate (should be ~95%: the definition of a 95% CI, demonstrated).

Extend the script: vary n (20, 50, 200, 1000) and true lift (0, +0.2 SD, +0.5 SD); for each combo record P(reject H0) — print the power table and highlight the cell where n=1000, lift=+0.2 SD is 'significant' (power -> 1) to make the practical-significance point concrete.

Add the peeking demo: simulate optional stopping (check p daily for 14 days, stop at first p<0.05 under TRUE null) over 2,000 runs; print the empirical false-positive rate (expect ~20-30%, not 5%) — the peeking inflation, measured.
Write the three takeaways as comments: what coverage means, why big-n significance is cheap, what peeking costs.

checks.output: coverage ~=0.95 printed; power table printed; peeking false-positive rate >> 0.05 printed
checks.hint: Vectorize the 1,000 experiments with numpy (shape (1000, n)) — loops will be slow; seed everything.

labs.debrief: You didn't read about coverage, power, and peeking — you measured them. Simulation turns abstract definitions into observed facts, which is why the lessons stick past exam day.

labs.title: Catch Simpson's Paradox
labs.objective: Construct a Simpson's paradox dataset and build the mix-check habit that defeats it.
steps: Generate the paradox with `python3` to /tmp/dsc_simpson.csv: two onboarding flows; flow B beats flow A within mobile AND within desktop, but flow B's aggregate is worse — engineer it via segment MIX (flow B gets far more desktop users, who convert lower overall).
Write `/tmp/dsc_simpson.py`: print the aggregate comparison ('B loses'), then the segmented comparison ('B wins everywhere'), then the MIX table (segment shares per flow) that explains the reversal.
Add the automated guard: a function `check_mix(df, group_col, segment_col)` that warns when segment shares differ by >10 points between groups — the dashboard-level defense against paradoxes.
Write the recommendation comment: which comparison is decision-valid (segmented/stratified) and what the team should do (ship B, and fix the assignment mix going forward).

checks.output: aggregate shows B worse, segments show B better, mix table explains it, guard function warns
checks.hint: Pick conversion rates like mobile 50%/48%, desktop 38%/35%, with mixes 30/70 vs 70/30 — the arithmetic must reverse the aggregate.

labs.debrief: You built a paradox on purpose, which means you'll recognize one in the wild. The mix-check is now part of your dashboard hygiene — aggregates don't get trusted without it.

labs.title: Run the Cert Decision Gates
labs.objective: Evaluate one real certification through the four-gate decision framework and write the verdict.
steps: Pick a certification you're actually considering; create `/tmp/dsc_cert_decision.md` with the four gates: GOAL (the specific role/outcome), AUDIENCE (evidence of recognition), GAP (what it proves that experience doesn't), COST (full cost incl. hours).

For AUDIENCE, do the real research: sample 20 target job postings (or LinkedIn role descriptions) and count explicit mentions — record the fraction; note whether the cert is required, preferred, or absent.
For COST, fill the ROI worksheet: fee + materials + (hours x your hour value); estimate P(pass) from a practice diagnostic if available, else state the assumption; compute expected value vs cost.
Write the VERDICT (GO / NO-GO / DEFER with conditions) plus the sequencing note (what comes before/after, which portfolio project pairs with it) — sign and date it.

checks.output: four gates filled with specific evidence (posting counts, hour math, P(pass)); verdict + sequencing present
checks.hint: Vague gates ('good for career') fail the exercise — every gate needs a number or a name.

labs.debrief: You replaced 'should I get certified?' vibes with a worksheet that kills bad certs at gate 1 and justifies good ones with arithmetic. Run every future credential through it.

labs.title: Generate Your 8-Week Plan
labs.objective: Build a real 8-week study plan from a diagnostic, with weighted allocation and checkpoints.
steps: Take (or simulate) a diagnostic: score yourself per exam domain (or use plausible numbers); write `/tmp/dsc_plan.py` that takes domain weights + diagnostic scores and outputs hour allocations via the weighted-gap formula: hours_i proportional to weight_i x (100 - score_i), reserving 15% for maintenance and 10% buffer.

Have the script print a week-by-week skeleton: weeks 1-2 foundations + diagnostic review, weeks 3-6 targeted depth (top weighted gaps first), week 7 integration + taper start, week 8 taper — with the three full-practice dates circled.

Add the Sunday-review template to the script's output: sensors (scores, breakdown), process check (% retrieval-based), actuator (reallocation), circuit breaker (energy, trend) — print it as a weekly checklist.
Run it on your numbers; save the printed plan to /tmp/dsc_study_plan.txt and note the single biggest reallocation the math prescribed versus your gut allocation.

checks.output: per-domain hour allocations printed (weighted-gap math); 8-week skeleton with practice dates; Sunday checklist; plan saved
checks.hint: Normalize allocations to your real weekly hours; the formula sets proportions, you set the total.

labs.debrief: Your plan is now arithmetic, not aspiration — every hour has a weighted-gap justification, and the Sunday review makes it adaptive. The gut-vs-math comparison usually reveals one big misallocation; you just fixed it.

labs.title: Start the Wrong-Answer Journal
labs.objective: Build a working wrong-answer journal with failure-kind classification and retest scheduling.
steps: Create `/tmp/dsc_journal.py`: a tiny CLI/CSV journal where each entry records question id, domain, your answer, correct answer, failure KIND (knowledge/parsing/trap/time), the one-sentence RULE ('paired + skewed + n=15 -> Wilcoxon'), and a retest date (+3 days).

Enter 10 real misses (from any practice set, or the scenario questions in this bootcamp — redo them and log honestly); the script must refuse entries without a kind and a rule (that's the discipline).
Add a `due` command listing entries due for retest, and a `report` command showing kind-ratios (e.g., 'parsing: 40%') — the sensor for whether your STUDY SYSTEM needs a parsing intervention.
Do one retest cycle on due items: re-answer from scratch, mark status; print the kind-ratio report and write the one system change it prescribes (if any).

checks.output: 10 entries logged; kind-ratios printed; due list works; at least one retest completed
checks.hint: Keep the rule to one sentence — if it needs a paragraph, you haven't understood the miss yet.

labs.debrief: Misses are now assets with retest dates, not regrets. The kind-ratio report is the highest-leverage 30 seconds in your prep — it tells you whether to study content or fix process.

labs.title: Read Your Score Trend
labs.objective: Analyze a practice-score history like a go/no-go instrument: margin, floors, trend.
steps: Create `/tmp/dsc_scores.csv` with 6 practice results: date, overall %, and per-domain %s (use realistic numbers — include one plateau stretch and one domain floor violation to make the analysis interesting).

Write `/tmp/dsc_trend.py`: load the CSV, plot (or print) the overall trend, compute the margin vs YOUR pass line + buffer target, flag any domain below the 70% floor, and classify the trend (rising/stable/falling/plateaued).

Implement the verdict function: GO only if (3 most recent >= target) AND (no domain < floor) AND (trend not falling); else output the branch plan (2-3-week targeted extension vs 4+-week rebuild + reschedule vs circuit-breaker rest).

Run it on your CSV; write the verdict paragraph as if 3 days before the exam — then deliberately tweak one input (drop the last score 6 points) and observe how the verdict changes: that's the rule working.

checks.output: trend classification, margin check, floor flags, and a GO/NO-GO verdict with branch plan printed
checks.hint: The verdict must be mechanical — if you find yourself overriding it, the rule needs the override written in, not ignored.

labs.debrief: You turned score history into a decision instrument with pre-committed gates. Exam-week you will thank present you — the rule decides so anxiety doesn't have to.

labs.title: Audit a README in 20 Seconds
labs.objective: Score a project README against the 20-second scan test and fix the top of the page.
steps: Pick one of your project repos (or a sample); open its README in a private window and start a 20-second timer — write down what a stranger learns: what it does, why it matters, the key result, how to run it.
Score it 0-4 (one point per question answered above the fold); write `/tmp/dsc_readme_audit.md` with the score, the exact line where each answer was found (or 'NOT FOUND'), and the fix for each miss.
Rewrite the top of the README using the skeleton: outcome headline, key visual with takeaway caption, 3-bullet results, 3-command run block, deep-dive link — keep it under 40 lines above the fold.
Re-run the 20-second test on the rewrite; record the new score. If still below 4/4, iterate once more — the test, not your taste, is the judge.

checks.output: before/after 20-second scores recorded; every miss has a named fix; rewrite present
checks.hint: Time yourself honestly — 20 seconds is shorter than you think, which is the point.

labs.debrief: The README is a landing page with a conversion metric, and you just learned to measure it. The 20-second test is now your pre-publish gate for every repo.

labs.title: Fresh-Clone Reproducibility
labs.objective: Prove a portfolio project reproduces from a fresh clone — or fix it until it does.
steps: Clone one of your project repos into a FRESH directory (or simulate with `cp -r` to /tmp/freshclone, deleting any local caches); create a clean virtualenv with `python3 -m venv /tmp/freshvenv`.

Follow ONLY the README's run instructions: install requirements, fetch data via the documented link/script, run the entry point — log every deviation, missing step, or error in `/tmp/dsc_repro_log.md`.
Fix the repo (not the log): pin requirements with ==, repair the data link or add a download script, remove hardcoded paths, set seeds — then repeat the fresh-clone test until it passes clean.
Write the reproducibility receipt in the README: exact commands, expected runtime, expected outputs (with hashes or key numbers) — the stranger should never have to guess.

checks.output: deviations logged per attempt; final attempt clean; receipt added to README
checks.hint: The most common failures: unpinned deps, dead data links, absolute paths — check those first.

labs.debrief: A project nobody can run is a project nobody trusts. The fresh-clone test is the only honest reproducibility check, and your flagship now passes it.

labs.title: Scan Postings for Cert Signal
labs.objective: Measure employer recognition of two certifications from real job-posting text.
steps: Collect 20-30 target job postings (copy the requirements/qualifications sections into /tmp/dsc_postings.txt, one per line, or use a small script with placeholder text you write from real postings you've seen).

Write `/tmp/dsc_scan.py`: for each of two candidate certs (plus 2-3 spelling variants each, e.g., 'AWS Certified Machine Learning', 'AWS ML Specialty'), count case-insensitive mentions; also count 'preferred' vs 'required' contexts via nearby keywords.

Print the scoreboard: mentions per cert, required-vs-preferred split, and the fraction of postings mentioning NEITHER (the 'experience-only' share) — then write the one-paragraph interpretation: which cert (if either) the market actually screens on.
Note the limitations in comments: sample bias (your 25 postings aren't the market), keyword vs real screening, and when you'd re-run the scan (before any cert purchase).

checks.output: mention counts per cert with variants; required/preferred split; interpretation paragraph
checks.hint: Normalize text (lowercase, strip punctuation) before matching; count postings-with-mention, not raw mention counts.

labs.debrief: 'Recognized by employers' is now a number from YOUR market, not a vendor's claim. Re-run the scan before every cert purchase — markets move.

labs.title: The Pacing Drill
labs.objective: Internalize per-question pacing with checkpoints on a timed 20-question set.
steps: Assemble 20 practice questions (any domain mix); build your pacing card for a 65-question/170-minute exam scaled down: budget = 2.6 min/q, cap 4 min, checkpoint at question 7 (~18 min) and 14 (~36 min).

Run the set under strict conditions: timer visible, whiteboard only, flag-and-return enforced mechanically at the 4-minute cap — log per-question times in `/tmp/dsc_pacing.csv` (question, seconds, flagged Y/N).
Write `/tmp/dsc_pacing_review.py`: load the CSV, report average time, count of cap-hits, checkpoint adherence (were you on pace at 7 and 14?), and blanks (must be zero — guess pass at the end).
Write the one adjustment for next time: the single pacing behavior to change (e.g., 'stop re-reading stems twice on calculation questions') — pacing improves one behavior at a time.

checks.output: avg time, cap-hits, checkpoint adherence, zero blanks confirmed, one behavior adjustment named
checks.hint: Be honest with the timer — pausing it 'just for a sec' trains the wrong reflex.

labs.debrief: Pacing is now a practiced skill with data, not a personality trait. The cap-and-flag reflex you built here is what saves exams at question 40.

labs.title: Distractor Autopsy
labs.objective: Dissect 10 hard questions by distractor archetype and name your personal kryptonite.
steps: Take 10 difficult practice questions you've missed or found hard; for each, create an entry in `/tmp/dsc_distractors.md`: the stem's planted key (the deciding fact), each distractor's archetype (TRUE-BUT-IRRELEVANT / EXTREME / HALF-RIGHT / TEXTBOOK-DEFAULT), and the differentiator that settled the final two.
Tally the archetypes: which one caught YOU most often? Write the pattern in one sentence (e.g., 'I pick the textbook-default when the stem plants a complication I skimmed').
Write the counter-drill for your top archetype: 5 new questions where you must FIRST name the archetype of each option before choosing — archetype-first, answer-second.
Re-answer the original 10 with the archetype lens; record how many flip to correct and what that says about knowledge vs test-craft gaps.

checks.output: 10 entries with planted keys, archetype labels per distractor, personal kryptonite named, counter-drill present
checks.hint: If every distractor feels 'random', you haven't found the misconception it encodes — dig one level deeper.

labs.debrief: Distractors stopped being 'tricky options' and became a taxonomy you can see through. Your kryptonite archetype is now a named, drilled weakness instead of a recurring surprise.

labs.title: Build the Spaced-Repetition Loop
labs.objective: Create a working spaced-repetition schedule for your weak topics, driven by the journal.
steps: List 15 topics/concepts from your wrong-answer journal (or the statistics-core lessons); write `/tmp/dsc_spaced.py` holding each as a card: front (prompt) / back (the one-sentence rule).

Implement the scheduler: intervals [1, 3, 7, 14, 30] days; each review grades recall (again/hard/good/easy) and moves the card forward/back on the ladder; the script prints today's due queue from a JSON state file.
Seed the state file with your 15 cards at staggered intervals (as if some were learned days ago); run the `due` command and complete one full review session, grading honestly.
Add the integration: a function that imports due journal retests into the queue — the journal and the spaced system are one loop, not two tools; print the combined queue.

checks.output: due queue printed from state file; review session completable; journal import works
checks.hint: Store state as JSON with next_due dates (ISO format); the script computes 'today' vs due — keep it simple, no libraries needed.

labs.debrief: Retention is now a designed loop, not a hope. The journal finds the gaps, the scheduler defends them against the forgetting curve — and the combined queue is your daily 15 minutes that compounds.

simulations.title: The significant result that wasn't
simulations.brief: The team ran an experiment, checked the dashboard daily, and stopped the moment p dipped below 0.05. The 'win' vanished on re-run.

steps.symptom: p=0.04 at the stopping day; the effect disappears on re-run.
evidence: Experiment log
Results checked on 12 separate days; the team stopped on day 12 when p hit 0.04
Sample size plan
None — no pre-registered sample size or stopping rule
Re-run
Identical setup, p=0.38
options: Pre-register the sample size and stopping rule; use a sequential test or correct for peeking
Run it a third time and average the p-values
Lower the bar to p<0.10 so the win counts
Blame the re-run on a different user cohort
steps.explain: Checking 12 times and stopping at the first p<0.05 is peeking — the false-positive rate of that procedure is far above 5%. Fix the procedure: fixed horizon, or a sequential method that accounts for interim looks.

simulations.debrief: A p-value is only valid under the procedure that produced it. Peeking inflates false positives; pre-registration and proper sequential methods keep the 5% promise honest.

simulations.title: Train/test mismatch
simulations.brief: The gradient boosting model hits 99% on training data and 71% on the test set. The gap is the diagnosis.

evidence: Model config
500 trees, max depth 30, no regularization, learning rate 0.3
Validation
Single 80/20 split, no cross-validation
Learning curves
Train error keeps falling while validation error climbs after 60 trees
options: Add regularization, tune with cross-validation, and stop on validation error
Train for 500 more trees to close the gap
Collect a bigger test set so the 71% looks more reliable
Switch to a deeper model to fit the training data faster
steps.explain: The learning curves are the smoking gun: validation error rising while train error falls is overfitting. Depth-30 trees with no regularization memorize. Regularize, cross-validate, and early-stop on validation.

simulations.debrief: Train/test gaps diagnose overfitting. Regularization, cross-validation, and early stopping close the gap — more capacity widens it.

simulations.title: Choose the statistical test
simulations.brief: You measured conversion for the same 200 users before and after a checkout redesign. Pick the right test.

steps.text: Paired before/after measurements on the same 200 users. Which test?

choices.label: Paired t-test on the per-user differences
choices.feedback: Correct: paired data needs a paired test — the per-user differences are the unit of analysis, which removes between-user noise.

choices.label: Chi-square test of independence
choices.feedback: Chi-square ignores the pairing — it treats before and after as independent groups and throws away the within-user information.

simulations.debrief: Match the test to the design: paired measurements get paired tests, categorical counts get chi-square, multiple groups get ANOVA. The design decides, not the data shape.

simulations.title: Run a clean A/B test
simulations.brief: Put the A/B test workflow in the order that keeps the result trustworthy.

items: Run the test to the pre-registered sample size
State the hypothesis and primary metric
Analyze once the sample size is reached
Randomize users into control and variant
Size the sample with a power analysis

simulations.debrief: Hypothesis first, power analysis before launch, randomization at assignment, run to the plan without peeking, analyze once. Skip any step and the p-value stops meaning what you think it means.

simulations.title: Review the study config
simulations.brief: A teammate's experiment plan. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).

steps.config:
hypothesis: new_checkout_raises_conversion
randomization: none
sample_size: 40
primary_metric: conversion_rate
stopping_rule: peek_daily
significance: 0.05

issues.description: No randomization — the variant effect is confounded with every pre-existing difference between the groups.
issues.fix: Randomize users into control and variant at assignment time.

issues.description: Peeking daily inflates the false-positive rate far above the stated 0.05.
issues.fix: Run to a pre-registered sample size or use a sequential testing method.

simulations.debrief: Two experiment-design killers: no randomization (confounding) and peeking (false positives). Randomize, pre-register, and run to the plan.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.

Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before

Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.

Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one

Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet

The measurable result of the prioritization

Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers

Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.

How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
